summary: Specifies implementation requirements for running RSVP over ATM switched virtual circuits, ensuring multiple implementations interoperate and conform to the RSVP and Integrated Services specifications.

eli5.summary: The must-follow rules so different makers' equipment can reserve space on ATM networks in the same way.

subtitle: The must-follow rules that let different vendors' RSVP routers set up QoS circuits over ATM and still interoperate.

tldr.problem: RSVP reservations are receiver-driven and can change at any time, while ATM circuits are set up by the sender and cannot change their QoS after setup, so independent implementations could easily fail to work together.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC fixes the points that must be common: the sender always opens the QoS circuits, RSVP control messages never share a QoS circuit with data, QoS changes are done by building a replacement circuit, and multicast circuits are managed so that every receiver gets the data.
tldr.outcome: Following these MUST-level rules lets implementations that choose different design options (described in the companion documents) still interoperate. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Control and data on one QoS VC

today: RFC 2380 is a Proposed Standard published in August 1998, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to be read with RFC 2379, RFC 2381 and RFC 2382.

sections.title: Scope and Assumptions
sections.content:
RFC 2380 covers running IP over ATM where switched virtual circuits (SVCs) carry QoS flows and RSVP is the internet-level QoS signaling protocol. It applies to the CLIP/ION, LANE 2.0 and MPOA methods of supporting IP over ATM, and it defines requirements for implementations using ATM UNI 3.x and 4.0. Every RSVP over ATM implementation must follow them to interoperate.

It is a companion to RFC 2379 (implementation guidelines) and RFC 2382 (the general framework), and the reader is expected to know both. The RFC also assumes RSVP as described in RFC 2205, either IPv4 or IPv6, and that best effort service keeps working. Permanent virtual circuits are treated like point-to-point links, so the memo assumes SVCs.

Two terms are pinned down. A reservation is an RSVP-initiated request for resources, triggered by RESV message processing (refresh-only RESV messages do not count). A flow is the data traffic for one reservation: one flow per session for shared styles, one per sender for distinct styles.
sections.eli5: Before the rules start, the RFC says what it is talking about: reserving a guaranteed lane on an ATM network. It also defines two words, so everyone means the same thing by them.

sections.title: Control Messages and VC Initiation
sections.content:
RSVP over ATM implementations MUST NOT send RSVP control messages on the same QoS VC as the RSVP-associated data packets. They MAY send them on the best effort data path or on a separate control VC. If the data VC fails and cannot be reestablished, RSVP SHOULD treat it as an allocation failure. If the VC carrying control messages is abnormally released and cannot be reestablished, the associated QoS VCs MUST also be released, to keep forwarding state and reservation state in sync.

RSVP is receiver oriented and ATM is sender oriented, but the RFC argues this is not a real problem: RESV requests come from the receiver, but resources are actually allocated at the subnet sender. So subnet senders MUST establish all QoS VCs, and RSVP-enabled subnet receivers MUST be able to accept incoming QoS VCs. This lets senders use different flow-to-VC mappings and renegotiation techniques without breaking interoperability.

Implementations MAY send data backwards on an RSVP-initiated point-to-point QoS VC, but it must conform to the backward traffic parameters. Since the initiator sets those, resources are quite likely not requested for the backward direction. Backward data is not available on point-to-multipoint VCs.
sections.eli5: The person who asks for the lane (the receiver) is not the one who builds it. The sender builds every reserved lane, and the receiver must be ready to accept it. Messages about the lanes travel on a different road than the cars.

sections.title: VC Teardown and Dynamic QoS
sections.content:
Ordinary IP-over-ATM VCs are torn down by inactivity timers because IP is connectionless. RSVP has its own explicit messages and timeouts, so data VCs set up for RSVP flows should be released only at RSVP's direction. This conflicts with RFC 1755, which recommends tearing down an inactive VC and suggests twenty minutes. The configurable inactivity timer MUST be set to infinite for RSVP-initiated VCs, and implementations MUST NOT use an inactivity timer to clear any received connection, which also matches the update to RFC 1755 in RFC 2331.

RSVP lets QoS change at any time, but ATM UNI 3.x and 4.0 allow no change after VC setup. The method is to replace the VC. While the replacement is being set up, the old VC MUST be left in place unmodified. Once the new one is up, data moves to it and only then is the old one closed.

If the replacement fails, the old VC keeps being used. If the new reservation is larger than the old one, the request MUST be answered with an error. If it is smaller, it MUST be treated as successful, leaving the larger allocation in place. Implementations SHOULD retry replacing a too-large VC after some time. Only one QoS change per reservation is processed at a time: if the request changes again mid-setup, the replacement SHOULD be released and the process restarted.
sections.eli5: An ATM lane cannot be made wider once it is built. So to change the size, you build a new lane first, move the traffic over, and only then close the old one. Nobody has to stop in the meantime.

sections.title: Encapsulation
sections.content: All RSVP over ATM implementations MUST be able to support LLC encapsulation per RFC 1483 on RSVP-triggered QoS VCs. They MAY negotiate alternative encapsulations using the B-LLI negotiation procedures of ATM signalling. When a QoS VC carries only IP packets, implementations SHOULD negotiate VC-based multiplexing, which avoids the overhead of the LLC header.
sections.eli5: Every parcel can travel in a standard labeled box that everyone understands. If the lane only carries one kind of parcel, you can skip the label and save space.

sections.title: Multicast Heterogeneity and Best Effort Receivers
sections.content:
In a multicast session, heterogeneity means receivers ask for different QoS levels, and some ask for none. RFC 2382 offers four models for dealing with it: full heterogeneity, limited heterogeneity, homogeneous, and modified homogeneous. Whichever model is used, implementations MUST NOT normally send more than one copy of a data packet to a given next-hop (ATM end-point). Brief duplicates during VC setup and transition are acceptable.

Implementations MUST also make sure data reaches best effort receivers, via best effort or QoS VCs as the model allows. They must not create VCs in a way that data cannot be sent to a best effort receiver, including not being able to add one to a QoS VC. Failure to set up best effort VCs is a general IP over ATM failure and out of scope.

When a RESV arrives from a new next-hop asking for more than any existing reservation, the dynamic QoS process SHOULD start first, and the new next-hop SHOULD be the first end-point of the new VC, which minimizes signaling if setup to that next-hop fails.
sections.eli5: If a group of friends wants the same video, some pay for the express lane and some do not. Everyone must still get the video, and nobody should get two copies, except briefly while the lanes are being built.

sections.title: Multicast End-Point Identification
sections.content:
Implementations must be able to identify the ATM end-points in an IP multicast group, both QoS and best effort ones. RSVP next-hop information usually provides the QoS end-points but not the best effort ones. A full list may be available from multicast over ATM control mechanisms such as MARS in mesh mode, or from multicast routing protocols. Comparing that list against the RSVP-identified end-points yields the best effort receivers.

A special case arises when a next-hop is not RSVP capable and RSVP is tunneled automatically. The RESV may reach the source by a different route than the PATH message, so the source does not know which ATM end-point goes with the reservation. This is harmless for unicast, where the end-point is the IP next-hop router, but multicast routing may not identify the next-hop router uniquely.

The preferred fix is multicast control mechanisms and routing protocols that identify end-points uniquely. Failing that, all IP routers used to support RSVP over ATM should support RSVP. To ensure proper behavior, baseline implementations MUST only establish RSVP-initiated VCs to RSVP capable end-points, though a user may be allowed to override this.
sections.eli5: To deliver to everyone in a group, you first need the guest list. Sometimes the list is incomplete, so the safe rule is to only build reserved lanes to guests who understand reservations.

sections.title: Multicast Distribution and Receiver Transitions
sections.content:
There are two models for multicast data over ATM. In mesh (VC mesh) mode, senders open point-to-multipoint VCs straight to all destinations. In server mode, senders use point-to-point VCs to a central multicast server, which relays onto point-to-multipoint VCs. Current multicast servers cannot be told about QoS requirements, so implementations SHOULD support mesh mode for RSVP-controlled multicast flows. If a server that cannot take QoS requests is used, the sender MUST set the service-specific break bit (not the global one), telling receivers the router supports RSVP and Integrated Services but the service cannot be delivered over this ATM network.

For MARS, distribution mode is set by administrators, who MUST configure mesh mode for groups used in RSVP sessions. For LANE 1.0 the only option is the Broadcast and Unknown Server, so the break bit MUST always be set. LANE 2.0 allows non-server solutions that may deliver proper QoS.

While a point-to-multipoint VC is being built, some receivers are on it and some are not. For a first QoS VC or a replacement VC, data MUST NOT be sent on the new VC until all parties have been added, so everyone receives each packet once. When adding an end-point to an existing QoS VC, the add MUST complete first and the drop from the best effort VC follows. This avoids data loss but means receivers must tolerate some duplicate packets during QoS setup.
sections.eli5: Either each sender delivers to everyone directly, or sends to a middleman who passes it on. The middleman cannot handle special lanes, so direct delivery is preferred. When changing lanes, make sure everyone is on the new one before you start, and join the new lane before leaving the old.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says that the same considerations stated in RFC 2205 and RFC 1755 apply, and that it raises no additional security issues.
sections.eli5: The RFC says it adds no new dangers beyond those already known for the two things it connects.
